name: Hypochlorous acid spray

lead: A hypochlorous acid (HOCl) spray is a mild antimicrobial mist used on skin. HOCl is the same chemical neutrophils make to kill microbes. Acne-prone users spray it to reduce bacteria and soothe irritation for calmer, clearer-looking skin.

HOCl oxidises microbial proteins and damages membranes. In one study, an HOCl eyelid solution cut staphylococci by over 99% in 20 minutes. Since 2016 the US FDA has cleared products with HOCl as the main active for wounds and infections. No studies of cosmetic outcomes such as acne were identified.

paras: People mist it onto cleansed skin, or onto the chest and back, once or twice a day, often after workouts or shaving and before moisturizer. It is used as a gentle add-on to an existing routine and is also common after procedures such as microneedling.
The EPA classes it as non-hazardous, though as an oxidiser it can irritate depending on concentration. Solutions degrade and lose potency with time, heat and light, so shelf life is short.

angle.text: Acne-prone users mist hypochlorous acid on face or body to reduce bacteria and soothe irritation, for calmer, clearer-looking skin. It has regulatory clearance and studies in wound and eyelid care.

lead: Hypochlorous acid (HOCl) spray is a mist containing a dilute solution of hypochlorous acid, a weak acid that forms when chlorine dissolves in water. It is sold as a gentle, skin-compatible antimicrobial for the face and body, and people use it as a quick spritz to keep skin clean and calm in pursuit of clearer-looking skin.[1]

HOCl is also made naturally in the body: neutrophils, a type of white blood cell, generate it through the enzyme myeloperoxidase to help destroy microbes.[1] Since early 2016 the US FDA has approved products whose main active ingredient is hypochlorous acid for treating wounds and various infections in people and pets, and it is also FDA-approved as a preservative for saline solutions.[1]

Its antimicrobial action comes from oxidation of microbial proteins, DNA, lipids and energy-producing systems, and in a clinical test it was found non-toxic and non-irritating to eye and skin.[1] No clinical studies of HOCl sprays for cosmetic outcomes such as acne or skin clarity were found; documented research concerns wound care and eyelid hygiene.

paras: Hypochlorous acid has the formula HOCl and exists in equilibrium with the hypochlorite anion; both act as oxidisers and are the main disinfecting species in chlorine solutions.[1] Sodium hypochlorite, the active ingredient of household bleach, is a related compound, whereas HOCl itself is the weak acid used in mists and eyelid and wound products.[1]

HOCl was discovered in 1834 by Antoine Jerome Balard, who also named it. It is easy to make but hard to keep stable, and cost-effective production of stable solutions for commercial use developed only in recent years; most hypochlorous acid water still has a short shelf life.[1]

HOCl reacts with many biomolecules. It oxidises sulfur-containing groups in proteins, causing cross-linking, and affects DNA, lipids and amino acids; proposed explanations for bacterial killing include inhibited glucose oxidation, depletion of adenine nucleotides, inhibited DNA replication and protein unfolding and aggregation, and the source notes these mechanisms are still discussed.[1]

Described uses are wound care, eyelid hygiene, and disinfection through sprays, wipes and aerosols.[1] A 2017 study reported that a saline eyelid solution preserved with HOCl cut staphylococci by over 99 percent after 20 minutes without changing the overall diversity of bacteria on the eyelids.[1] A 2025 case report of refractory dry eye lists a hypochlorous acid spray among earlier treatments that gave limited relief.[2]
Skin-care sprays apply the same chemistry as a daily mist for the face and body. Because the molecule is made by the body's own immune cells, products are positioned as gentle on skin.

The US EPA classifies HOCl as non-hazardous, although as an oxidiser it can be corrosive or irritating depending on concentration and pH; a clinical test of hypochlorous acid water found it non-toxic and non-irritating to eyes and skin.[1] Solutions lose potency over time, and storage away from heat and direct sunlight slows deterioration.[1]
No studies found for appearance or acne outcomes of HOCl sprays. Related research includes the 2017 eyelid hygiene study and clinical use in wound care and infections.[1][2]
